title: Topic Drill: Reading Literary Passages (Set A)

items.stem:
The Alder Street Quilt Guild met on Thursdays in the back room of the library, where the radiator knocked and the coffee tasted of tin. Bernice had been piecing the same wedding-ring pattern for eleven years, ripping out seams whenever a corner failed to meet. Tonight the younger members held up her unfinished top and said it was already beautiful. She frowned at the puckered corners, then at the faces, and finally laid the quilt across her knees. ‘Finished is a kind of leaving,’ she said, ‘and I am not ready to leave this room.’

Which theme is best supported by the passage?
options: Careful craftsmanship always deserves to be praised by younger people
Traditional crafts are disappearing because few people still practice them
Unfinished work can keep a person tied to a community of friends
Mistakes in a pattern should be corrected as soon as they are seen
items.explanation: The guild members call the quilt beautiful, yet Bernice keeps it unfinished and says finishing is a kind of leaving, which ties her work to her place in the room. The theme is staying connected through ongoing work. Praise is not the point, the passage never says crafts are vanishing, and she is the one who refuses to fix her puckered corners.

items.stem:
Dr. Okafor’s chemistry lab at Brindle Community College had no windows, which suited Priya, who preferred measuring to talking. She labeled every beaker twice, once on the glass and once in her notebook. When her lab partner, Tomas, spilled his sample and braced for a scolding, Priya slid her own spare vial across the bench and returned to her pipette. ‘Mine is the same concentration,’ she murmured. ‘I checked it twice.’ Tomas stared at her for a moment, then at the labels, and began to laugh.

Which pair of words best describes Priya?
options: Anxious and rude
Carefree and boastful
Lonely and bitter
Exacting and quietly generous
items.explanation: Priya labels everything twice, which shows she is exacting, and she hands Tomas her own vial without a lecture, which shows quiet generosity. Anxious and rude does not fit her calm offer. Carefree and boastful contradicts her habit of checking twice, and lonely and bitter is unsupported when Tomas laughs and she keeps helping him.

items.stem:
By the third week of the season, the Thursday under-twelve league had settled into its habits. Coach Ramsey’s team lost every match, and every match ended the same way: the children shook hands, then ran to the fence where a man in a gray cap held out orange slices. He never shouted instructions. He never asked the score. Today, when Ivo finally kicked a goal into his own net, the man in the gray cap was the first to cheer.

What can be inferred about the man in the gray cap?
options: He values the children’s enjoyment over the result
He is the referee and must remain neutral about every goal
He is disappointed that the team keeps losing
He is a new coach who plans to change the lineup
items.explanation: The man hands out orange slices after every loss, never shouts instructions, never asks the score, and cheers for a goal kicked into the wrong net. Those habits show he values enjoyment over winning. A referee would not run a snack table, no disappointment appears, and a new coach would give directions, which he never does.

items.stem:
At six in the morning, Hollis clipped his harness to the rail and descended beneath the Marren Street bridge. Frost furred the steel. Below him the river moved slowly, gray and without a sound, and every bolt he tapped answered with the same dull note. He worked methodically, calling measurements to the empty air, aware that his own breath was the loudest thing for a mile. Somewhere above, the first truck crossed, and the whole span shivered once.

Which words best describe the mood of the passage?
options: Cheerful and lively
Hushed and watchful
Bitter and resentful
Playful and carefree
items.explanation: Frost, a silent gray river, dull notes from each bolt, and a breath that is the loudest sound for a mile create a hushed, watchful mood. Cheerful and lively ignores the silence. Bitter and resentful gives Hollis a feeling the text never states, and playful and carefree conflicts with his methodical, careful work under the bridge.

items.stem:
Nobody asked me whether I wanted the night rounds at the Dunmere water plant, but the schedule had my name on it, so I walked the catwalks alone, reading gauges by headlamp. The settling tanks lay flat and black. I told myself I was not afraid of them. Behind me a pump cycled on, and I gripped the rail and counted to ten, as if counting were a kind of work.

From which point of view is the passage told?
options: First person, from a worker’s own perspective
Third person limited, following only the plant supervisor around the grounds
Third person omniscient, entering the mind of every worker on the shift
Second person, speaking directly to a reader who is touring the plant
items.explanation: The narrator says ‘I walked,’ ‘I told myself’ and ‘Behind me,’ so the account is first person and limited to one worker’s own fear and thoughts. Third person would use he or she for the speaker. Omniscient narration would enter other minds, and second person would address the reader as you, which never happens here.

items.stem:
In the pottery studio on Alcott Row, the wheel hummed like a patient bee. Rosalind pressed her thumbs into the spinning clay, and the lump rose into a wall, thin as an eyelid, then sagged and folded in on itself. ‘Clay remembers every hurry,’ her teacher said. Rosalind scraped the ruin into the bucket, where it lay like a drowned bird, and began again with slower hands.

Which phrase is a simile that suggests the slumped clay is ruined and lifeless?
options: the wheel hummed like a patient bee
where it lay like a drowned bird
Clay remembers every hurry
a wall, thin as an eyelid
items.explanation: The slumped clay is compared to a drowned bird with the word like, so it is a simile, and the image of a drowned bird suggests something lifeless. The bee comparison is a simile about sound. The thin-as-an-eyelid phrase is a simile about delicacy. The remembering clay is personification, not a comparison about ruin.

items.stem:
The night nurse at Corrin Hospital moved with a deliberate calm, never rushing, never wasting a step. At three a.m., when the ward’s lone monitor began to chirp, she crossed the floor in seconds and silenced it with a touch. The new orderly, who had spent the evening nervously alphabetizing supply shelves, watched her with open envy. ‘Don’t fret over it,’ she told him, handing him a mug. ‘You will not feel so clumsy by spring.’

In the passage, the word deliberate most nearly means which of the following?
options: intentionally cruel
easily distracted
carefully planned and unhurried
willing to argue at length
items.explanation: Context shows the nurse never rushes and never wastes a step, so deliberate means careful and unhurried. Intentionally cruel fits an unrelated sense of intent and clashes with her kindness to the orderly. Easily distracted contradicts her focus at the monitor, and willing to argue confuses the word with debating, which has no place in a calm ward.

items.stem:
The ferry left Marrow Point at seven. Before it, there had been the long argument with her sister about the sale of the house, the cold coffee, the signing at the lawyer’s. During the crossing, Anneli stood at the stern watching the wake widen, and the quarrel dissolved into foam. By the time the island appeared, small and green, she was thinking only of the garden she would plant.

How does the order of events contribute to the meaning of the passage?
options: Events are told in random order to confuse the reader
A flashback replaces the main action of the crossing
The ending returns to the argument to restore tension
It traces Anneli’s shift from past conflict toward hope
items.explanation: The passage first recalls the quarrel, the cold coffee and the signing, then moves through the crossing to the island and the garden, so the order tracks Anneli’s shift from conflict to hope. The events are not random. No flashback replaces the crossing, and the ending moves forward to the garden rather than returning to the argument.

items.stem:
Dear Margit, the quilt arrived on Tuesday, and I laid it across the bed before I dared read your note. Every square is one of the cotton shirts Papa wore at the bakery, you wrote, and I traced the faded stripes with my finger until the light went. I had thought I had forgotten how he looked at the end of a shift, floury to the elbows. Now I can almost smell the yeast. Thank you for the parcel, and for the stamps you tucked inside.

Which sentence best supports the idea that the quilt revives the writer’s memories?
options: Every square is one of the cotton shirts Papa wore at the bakery.
Thank you for the parcel, and for the stamps you tucked inside.
Now I can almost smell the yeast.
I laid it across the bed before I dared read your note.
items.explanation: The sentence about smelling the yeast shows the quilt bringing back a sensory memory of the father, which is the revival itself. The sentence about the shirts only tells what the quilt is made of. The thanks for the parcel is a courtesy, and laying the quilt on the bed describes a delay before reading, not a memory.

items.stem:
The league committee had voted, again, to move the final to a field with no lights. Gabriela read the announcement twice, folded it into a square, and tucked it into her shin guard. ‘Fine,’ she told the empty bench. ‘We will play in the dark, then.’ She laced her cleats with a tug that could have snapped the strings. Nobody heard her, which was exactly why she said it so loudly.

Which tone does Gabriela’s speech convey?
options: Gentle resignation
Playful excitement
Idle curiosity
Bitter defiance
items.explanation: Gabriela folds the announcement, tugs her laces hard enough to nearly snap them, and speaks loudly to an empty bench, which shows bitter defiance. Gentle resignation does not match the hard tug. Playful excitement is contradicted by the clipped ‘Fine.’ Idle curiosity is unsupported because she reads the news with plain frustration, not wonder.

items.stem:
In the winter of 1893 the telegraph office at Corliss Junction stayed open all night, though no message had come in nine days. Operator Pruett oiled the key, swept the floor, and wrote the weather in the log. When at last the sounder clattered, he did not leap up. He sat with his hand on the desk, listening to the whole line speak, as a man listens to rain after a long drought.

Which theme is most strongly developed in the passage?
options: Technology will always replace human workers eventually
Faithfulness endures through long stretches of silence
Winter weather makes communication nearly impossible
Lonely jobs ought to be avoided by sensible people
items.explanation: Pruett keeps the office open, oils the key and logs the weather through nine silent days, and when the message comes he listens rather than leaps. Together these show faithfulness enduring through silence. Nothing suggests machines replacing workers, the winter is never said to block messages, and the passage does not argue that such jobs should be avoided.

items.stem:
My uncle ran the crossing at Veldt Ferry for thirty years, and his praise came as grudgingly as a coin from a miser. When I finally steered the boat into the slip without a bump, he only nodded at the rope and said, ‘Tie it better.’ But that evening I found him telling the dockhands, loudly, that the boy had good hands.

In the passage, the word grudgingly most nearly means which of the following?
options: unwillingly, with reluctance
freely and without limit
with obvious cruelty
very loudly
items.explanation: The comparison to a coin from a miser shows praise that was held back, so grudgingly means unwillingly or with reluctance. Freely and without limit is the opposite of the miser image. With obvious cruelty overstates his gruffness, since he later brags about the boy. Very loudly describes his evening talk, not the way the praise first came.

items.stem:
At four in the morning the loading bay of the Harcourt bakery was already warm. Luz wiped flour from her glasses and checked the clipboard: forty trays, same as yesterday. A single small lunch bag sat unopened on the shelf, beside a child’s drawing of a sun with a smiling face, taped there crooked. She did not look at it. She counted the trays again.

What can the reader most reasonably infer about Luz?
options: She is annoyed that the bakery owner is late
She is working while longing for her family
She is hungry but has forgotten her own lunch
She is unsure that the tray count is right
items.explanation: The child’s drawing, the untouched lunch bag, and her refusal to look at them while she counts trays again suggest Luz is working at night while missing her child. Annoyance at an owner is never mentioned. Forgotten hunger ignores the drawing, and the count is the same as yesterday, so her counting again is avoidance, not doubt.

items.stem:
The kiln breathes out its heat at dawn, and the shelves of bowls wait like gray moons for their glaze. Marta lifts one into the light. It rings when she flicks it, a small, clear bell, and she thinks of all the hands that have carried fire into clay since the first potter lit a pit in the dark.

What does the comparison of the bowls to gray moons suggest?
options: They are round, pale and waiting to be finished
They are cold and unwelcome to the potter
They are too fragile to survive the glaze
They are glowing brightly from inside the kiln
items.explanation: A moon is round and pale, and the bowls are gray and still waiting for glaze, so the comparison suggests roundness and an unfinished state. Marta lifts one and hears it ring, so it is not unwelcome. A clear bell tone suggests soundness rather than fragility, and gray bowls waiting on shelves are not glowing.

items.stem:
The guild’s president, Orla, believed no one noticed how often she checked the door. Across the room, Dessa noticed. She also noticed that the chair beside Orla had stood empty since her husband’s funeral, and that Orla kept her handbag on it so nobody would ask to sit there. Dessa said nothing. She simply carried her own chair across and set it down, close enough to share the lamp.

Which statement best describes the point of view of the passage?
options: Third person limited, restricted entirely to what Orla thinks and sees
First person, told by Dessa as she remembers the evening afterward
Third person omniscient, entering the minds of both women
Second person, addressing the reader as the guild’s grieving president
items.explanation: The narrator uses he and she, so the voice is third person, and it reveals what Orla believed as well as what Dessa noticed, so it enters both minds. It is therefore not limited to Orla. No I appears to mark a first-person narrator, and no you addresses the reader, which rules out second person.

items.stem:
Field notes, Tuesday. Pier 3 shows hairline cracking along the east face; widest measure 2 mm. I photographed each crack and marked the ends with chalk. Pier 4 is sound. By afternoon the chalk had run in a light drizzle, and I will return with paint tomorrow. Note to self: the drizzle will wash away more than chalk if the cracking is as deep as I fear.

What is the effect of the final sentence of the passage?
options: It summarizes the findings for the pier’s builders
It corrects an error made in the earlier measurements
It introduces a new, unrelated inspection site
It adds a personal worry to an otherwise plain record
items.explanation: Until the last line the notes are flat records of cracks, photographs and chalk. The closing note says the writer fears the cracking may be deep, which adds personal worry. It does not summarize findings for builders, it corrects no measurement, and it stays with Pier 3 and the drizzle rather than naming a new site.

items.stem:
Coach Imelda never raised her voice. When the striker, a boy named Joss, missed the open net in the final minute, the whole bench groaned. She walked over, crouched in front of him, and retied his lace, which had come undone. ‘Next season,’ she said, ‘you will remember how this feels, and it will make you braver, not smaller.’ Then she stood and shouted, cheerfully, for the team to get oranges.

What does Coach Imelda’s response reveal about her?
options: She secretly blames him for losing the match
She encourages him instead of blaming him
She cares only about the team trophy
She is embarrassed by how the bench behaved
items.explanation: Imelda kneels, reties his lace and tells Joss the memory will make him braver, not smaller, which shows she encourages rather than blames. Secret blame is contradicted by her kindness. Caring only about a trophy ignores her focus on his feelings, and nothing shows she is embarrassed by the bench, since she simply moves on cheerfully.

items.stem:
Operator Delgado held the sample jar to the lamp. The water that morning was turbid, clouded with silt after the storm, and the readout on the turbidity meter agreed with his eyes. He logged the number, opened the secondary filter, and watched through the sight glass as the cloud slowly thinned, grain by grain, until the jar he filled an hour later sat clear as window glass.

In the passage, the word turbid most nearly means which of the following?
options: muddy and unclear
unusually warm
safe for drinking
strongly flavored
items.explanation: The passage defines turbid right away as clouded with silt, and the water later becomes clear as window glass, so turbid means muddy and unclear. Nothing says the water was warm. Safe for drinking is the opposite of a sample that needs more filtering, and flavor is never discussed since the reading depends on sight.

items.stem:
The ferry’s deckhand, Teague, announced every landing in the same flat voice, but when the boat docked at Selwick he lowered his clipboard and stared up at the cottages on the hill. Three summers ago, he told a passenger, he had left the island with one suitcase and a promise to return by spring. Nobody had asked him the date of the promise.

Which detail best supports the inference that Selwick holds personal meaning for Teague?
options: He announces every landing in a flat, unchanging voice throughout the day
He is carrying a clipboard as he works on the deck of the ferry
He lowers his clipboard and stares at the hill, then mentions leaving
He serves as a deckhand on a ferry that crosses the water all summer
items.explanation: Only at Selwick does Teague pause, stare at the hill and speak of leaving the island with a promise, which signals personal meaning. His flat announcements are how he treats every landing. The clipboard and his job describe his routine work and would be true at any stop, so they cannot show a special tie to one place.

items.stem:
The security guard at the Pellam Mill made his rounds at midnight, flashlight swinging, whistling off-key to keep the silence from settling on his shoulders. Dust turned over in the beam like slow snow. In the weaving hall, a single loom stood threaded, its half-finished cloth pale in the dark, as if the workers had stepped out for a moment and might return. He whistled louder.

Why does the author end the passage with the guard whistling louder?
options: To suggest he has finally discovered the missing workers
To show how he fights off the eerie silence
To show he is eager for the mill’s loom to be repaired
To prove that he enjoys music more than his duties
items.explanation: The guard already whistles to keep silence from settling on him, and the threaded loom makes the dark hall seem haunted, so whistling louder shows him pushing back against the eerie quiet. He finds no workers, the loom is half-finished rather than broken, and his whistling is a nervous habit, not proof of a preference for music.

items.stem:
On the rock called Gannet Stair, the lighthouse keeper polished the great lens each evening, though the new radio beacons had made the old light nearly useless. Ships passed in the dark without a glance. One October night a fishing boat, its radio dead, crept toward the rocks, and the beam swung across its bow like an open hand. In the morning the fishermen left a crate of mackerel at the keeper’s door and said nothing, for nothing was needed.

Which theme is best supported by the passage?
options: New inventions are always worse than older ones
Fishermen should avoid rocky coastlines at night
Generous gifts should be accepted without any comment
Steady work can matter most when no one expects it
items.explanation: The keeper keeps polishing a lens that seems useless, and when a boat with a dead radio nears the rocks the beam saves it, so steady work matters when least expected. The passage does not claim new inventions are worse, since the beacons simply failed this one boat. Nothing advises avoiding the coast, and the silent gift is a result, not the lesson.

items.stem:
Everyone in Fenwick Orchard agreed that old Mr. Abara talked too much about pears. He explained pears to the pickers, to the delivery drivers, to a salesman who had only wanted directions. But when frost threatened in April, it was Abara who walked the rows at midnight, lighting smudge pots one by one, and when his niece offered to take over he said, ‘No, no, I know these trees by name.’

What does Abara’s behavior reveal about his character?
options: He is talkative but deeply devoted to his trees
He is lazy and tries to leave hard work to others
He is secretive about how he grows his fruit
He is rude to every stranger who visits
items.explanation: Abara chatters about pears, yet he walks the rows at midnight lighting smudge pots and refuses help because he knows the trees by name, which shows talkative devotion. Laziness is contradicted by his night work. He shares his pear knowledge freely, so he is not secretive, and explaining things to a salesman is wordy, not rude.

items.stem:
WKLM went off the air at midnight, but Dario stayed in the booth until two. He cued records for no one, set the volume low, and read the dedications that had arrived by mail that week: a birthday for a trucker in Harlan, an anniversary at a diner, a get-well message for ‘the lady who sings in the laundromat.’ When the last card was read, he switched off the mic and sat for a while in the hum of the dark transmitter.

What can be inferred about Dario’s attitude toward his work?
options: He is waiting to be promoted to the morning show
He is staying late because the station owes him extra pay
He finds the mail tiresome and wants to finish quickly
He sees it as a way to stay connected to listeners
items.explanation: After the station is off the air, Dario still reads every card for listeners he cannot hear, which suggests he values the connection itself. No promotion is mentioned. Unpaid hours are never raised, and reading every dedication aloud, then sitting quietly with the transmitter, contradicts the idea that he finds the mail tiresome.

items.stem:
By dusk the Linden Square market had begun to fold itself away. Vendors snapped tarps over crates of quince and walnuts, and the smell of roasted chestnuts drifted between the stalls. A girl swung a paper lantern from her wrist, and its glow slid over the wet cobbles like warm honey. Somewhere a fiddle was tuning, then trying a tune, then stopping to laugh at itself.

Which mood does the passage create?
options: Tense and threatening
Bleak and abandoned
Warm and companionable
Solemn and mournful
items.explanation: The roasted chestnuts, the lantern glowing like warm honey and the fiddle that laughs at itself create a warm, companionable mood. Tense and threatening has no support. Bleak and abandoned ignores the lively vendors and the girl, and solemn and mournful clashes with the laughing fiddle and the cheerful end of a market day.

items.stem:
The summer I turned nine, my mother worked the ticket booth at the Halvorsen ice rink, and I learned to skate in the hours when nobody was watching. I fell, mostly. I remember the rubber mats and the cold that crept up my sleeves, and I remember how she would lean out of the booth window and clap, once, as if I had done something worthy of a stadium.

What does the narrator’s point of view allow the passage to do?
options: Reveal what the mother privately thinks of her job at the booth
Share direct memories and personal feelings
Report the events with no personal feeling at all
Show the rink through the eyes of several skaters at once
items.explanation: The narrator says I fell, I remember and my mother, so the first-person view lets the passage share direct memories and feelings, such as the cold in the sleeves and the single clap. It cannot reveal the mother’s private thoughts, it is full of personal feeling, and it never shifts to other skaters’ views.

items.stem:
The archive at the Wexcombe Library sleeps most of the year, its boxes breathing dust in the dim. When Sunita pulled a drawer open, the whole room seemed to sigh. Letters tied with brittle ribbon whispered against one another as she lifted them, and the old ledgers leaned on each other like tired travelers. She worked quietly, afraid to wake what they were dreaming.

Which technique is most prominent in the passage?
options: Hyperbole, exaggerating an ordinary detail for humor
Alliteration, repeating initial consonant sounds
Irony, saying the opposite of what is meant
Personification, giving objects human traits
items.explanation: The archive sleeps, boxes breathe, the room sighs, letters whisper and ledgers dream, so objects are given human traits, which is personification. No ordinary detail is exaggerated for laughs. Alliteration is not the dominant device, and irony would need statements that mean the opposite of what they say, which never happens here.

items.stem:
The busker on the Calder Street platform played a battered cello and kept a hat for coins. Some nights it held only a few pennies, a meager harvest for six hours of playing. Yet she bowed each tune as if the hall were full, and when an old man dropped in a button, she nodded gravely, as though it were gold.

In the passage, the word meager most nearly means which of the following?
options: small and far from enough
surprisingly generous
carefully counted
unexpectedly heavy
items.explanation: The hat holds only a few pennies after six hours of playing, so meager means small and inadequate. Surprisingly generous is the opposite, and the old man’s button is treated as a rare gift. Carefully counted is not suggested, and a few pennies could never be unexpectedly heavy, so the context rules that choice out.

items.stem:
Nine years after the flood, the town of Marlow held a ceremony at the water treatment plant. The mayor spoke about resilience. Behind her, an old operator named Lucian stood by the outflow, remembering the night the intake pipes failed and he had carried bottled water door to door in a wheelbarrow. At the end of the speech, the crowd applauded, and Lucian looked at the clean water and applauded too.

How does the shift from the mayor’s speech to Lucian’s memory contribute to the passage?
options: It shows the mayor and the operator disagree about the flood
It slows the plot so the reader forgets the ceremony
It sets public praise against one worker’s private experience
It reveals that the intake pipes are failing again
items.explanation: The mayor’s speech offers public praise, then the passage moves to Lucian’s wheelbarrow of bottled water, a private memory, so the shift contrasts the two. No disagreement appears since Lucian applauds. The ceremony frames the whole passage and is not forgotten, and the pipe failure belongs to the past flood rather than the present.

items.stem:
Because of her trembling hands, Odessa had given up painting. Glazing, however, was forgiving. A tremor became texture, and a wobble in the line became a ripple like water. Her teacher noticed the new pieces on the shelf and asked what had changed. ‘I stopped fighting the shake,’ she said, and glazed another bowl.

Which sentence best supports the idea that Odessa has made peace with her limitation?
options: Because of her trembling hands, Odessa had given up painting.
‘I stopped fighting the shake,’ she said.
Glazing, however, was forgiving.
Her teacher noticed the new pieces on the shelf and asked what had changed.
items.explanation: Odessa’s own words say she stopped fighting the tremor, which directly shows acceptance. The first sentence states the loss that caused her to give up painting. The sentence about glazing describes the craft, not her attitude. The teacher’s question only shows that something changed, not what Odessa feels about it.

items.stem:
The vending machine on the third floor and I have an understanding: I feed it coins and it keeps them. Tonight it offered me a single bag of pretzels, stale, and a look I can only call smug. I thanked it politely. At two in the morning one learns to respect any colleague who is consistent.

Which tone does the narrator convey?
options: Genuine gratitude
Deep anger
Dry humor
Fearful hesitation
items.explanation: The narrator treats a machine as a smug colleague, thanks it politely and praises its consistency, all with a straight face, which is dry humor. Genuine gratitude is mocked by the stale pretzels. Deep anger would use harsher words than ‘understanding,’ and nothing in the narrator’s tone suggests fear or hesitation.

items.stem:
Every night at the Verrin textile mill, Hanne left one lamp burning above the door of the dye house, though the foreman had twice ordered it dark to save oil. ‘Somebody might need to find their way back,’ she said. The workers laughed and rolled their eyes. But on the night the river rose and the lower road vanished under brown water, three of them followed that small yellow light up the hill and came home.

What does the lamp most likely symbolize?
options: The foreman’s stubborn authority over the workers
The mill’s wasteful spending on oil and supplies
The constant danger of the rising river
Guidance and care for others
items.explanation: Hanne keeps the lamp lit so somebody can find the way back, and during the flood it guides three workers home, so it stands for guidance and care. The foreman wants it dark, so it cannot stand for his authority. The oil is a cost he mentions, not the lamp’s meaning, and the river is the danger the lamp helps them escape.

items.stem:
Inspector Voss had spent thirty years warning towns about neglected bridges. On the morning of his retirement party he arrived early, parked beneath the old footbridge behind the town hall, and stood admiring the cake the staff had baked. Then a plank of the footbridge’s railing, rotted through, dropped onto the hood of his car.

Which statement best describes the irony in the passage?
options: His car is damaged by the neglect he warned about
He is honored with a retirement party and cake by the town
He arrives early and finds that no one has prepared
He is unable to retire because the footbridge needs repair
items.explanation: The irony is that a man who spent thirty years warning about neglected bridges has his own car struck by a rotted railing from one. The party and cake are the occasion, not the ironic twist. Nobody is unprepared, since the staff baked the cake, and nothing says his retirement is delayed by repairs.

items.stem:
Wren had booked the six o’clock ferry to start a job in the city, but fog held every boat at the dock. Her phone buzzed twice: the employer, then her mother. She watched the gray water, rehearsing the speech she would give if the island let her go, and the speech she would give if it did not. Neither felt true. When the horn finally sounded, she was still standing on the same plank.

Which conflict is central to the passage?
options: Wren against a rival who wants the same city job
Wren against a captain who refuses to sail in the fog
Wren’s inner struggle over leaving home
A storm threatening to sink the ferry at sea
items.explanation: Wren rehearses two speeches, one for leaving and one for staying, and neither feels true, so the main conflict is inside her over whether to leave home. No rival for the job appears. The fog delays the boats but no captain refuses her, and no storm threatens the ferry at sea.

items.stem:
In the back row of the biology lab, Mr. Dunmore, sixty-one, wrote lecture notes in a careful hand, the only student without a laptop. Classmates half his age politely ignored him during the first week. By the fifth week, three of them were asking to borrow his notes, and two stayed after class to hear him explain the Krebs cycle with a coffee ring and a pencil.

What does the passage suggest about the author’s attitude toward Mr. Dunmore?
options: Mocking, since he will not use new technology
Respectful, since he earns his classmates’ regard
Pitying, since his classmates still shun him
Indifferent, since his role in the lab is minor
items.explanation: The author shows Mr. Dunmore’s careful notes winning borrowers and listeners by week five, which presents him with respect. Mocking is contradicted by the classmates’ growing interest. Pitying fails because they no longer ignore him, and indifferent is unlikely when the passage follows his rise in standing in detail.

items.stem:
At the Corrie Pass hut, the logbook records weather, boots and blisters, but the one entry the wardens read aloud each spring dates from 1974: ‘Left a pot of soup on the stove. If you eat it, wash the pot.’ Climbers have added a line beneath it every year since, in many languages, and the page has swollen with thanks.

Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: A small act of kindness grew into a tradition
Climbers regularly ignore the rules about washing pots
The logbook matters mainly for its weather records
The wardens read entries aloud to teach safety
items.explanation: A single note about soup in 1974 has been answered by climbers in many languages every year, so a small kindness grew into a tradition. The note asks climbers to wash the pot, and nothing says they ignore it. The weather records are mentioned only in passing, and the wardens read this entry for its warmth, not to teach safety.

items.stem:
The greenhouse ring of Station Tallow turned slowly, and Iseult tended the tomatoes by hand, though the machines could have done it. Each morning she weighed the fruit and set aside the ripest, and when the supply drone arrived she sent those down the line unlabeled. The newest crew members ate them, fumbling with their trays and grateful for something sweet, never knowing whose they were.

What can be inferred about Iseult’s motive?
options: She is hurrying to dispose of spoiled fruit
She hopes the commander will reward her
She believes the drone cannot be trusted
She wants to welcome newcomers without credit
items.explanation: Iseult picks the ripest fruit and sends it unlabeled to the newest crew, who never learn the giver, so she is welcoming them without seeking credit. The fruit is ripest, not spoiled. Because it is unlabeled, she cannot be seeking a reward, and she uses the drone herself, so she does not distrust it.

items.stem:
Grief, for Tomasz, was a coat three sizes too large. He wore it to the bakery, to the bus, to his sister’s wedding, where it caught on every doorframe. Only in spring, when he found that the pocket held a button from his father’s shirt, did the sleeves begin to seem shorter.

What does the metaphor of the oversized coat suggest about Tomasz’s grief?
options: It is heavy and awkward to carry everywhere
It is a fashionable weight that others envy
It was caused by a mistake in tailoring
It disappears the moment he leaves his home
items.explanation: The coat is too large, goes everywhere with him and snags on doorframes, so it suggests a grief that is heavy and awkward. Nothing suggests others envy it. The tailoring is part of the image, not the cause of his grief, and he wears it out of the house to the bus and a wedding.

items.stem:
The new technician was reticent at the Monday briefing at the water plant, answering each question in a single word and studying the table instead of the faces. Her supervisors wondered whether she had been hired by mistake. By Friday, when a pump failed and the printed manual proved useless, she finally spoke up and laid out a full, precise plan for the repair.

In the passage, the word reticent most nearly means which of the following?
options: eager to take charge of every discussion
openly angry with the supervisors
reluctant to speak freely
easily bored by routine meetings
items.explanation: The technician answers in single words and looks at the table, so reticent means reluctant to speak freely. The contrast with her full plan on Friday confirms the meaning. Eager to take charge is the opposite of her Monday behavior. Nothing shows anger, and boredom is not suggested by her careful silence.

items.stem:
The deckhands treated Mrs. Quill like cargo, steering her gently to a bench and fetching blankets. She thanked them, waited until the ferry left the slip, then rose, walked to the wheelhouse, and corrected the captain’s heading by a few degrees. ‘Forty years on this water,’ she said mildly, ‘and the current still turns left at the buoy.’ The captain, to his credit, adjusted.

Which detail best shows that Mrs. Quill is not as helpless as the crew assumes?
options: She thanks the deckhands for fetching the blankets
She waits for the ferry to leave the slip
She sits on the bench the crew selected
She corrects the captain’s heading using her knowledge of the current
items.explanation: Mrs. Quill’s correction of the heading, backed by forty years of knowing the current, shows she is capable and expert. Thanking the deckhands is only politeness. Waiting for the ferry to depart and sitting where she was steered are the ordinary things the crew expects, so none of them shows hidden strength.

items.stem:
Experiment 14 failed. So did 15. By Experiment 22, the whiteboard in Room 204 was a thicket of crossed-out hypotheses, and Professor Lind had stopped erasing them. ‘Failures are data with better manners,’ she told the class, tapping the board. The students laughed, but several copied the line into their notebooks.

Why does the author open with short sentences about failed experiments?
options: To show that the students dislike the class
To stress repeated failure before a hopeful view
To explain how the experiments were designed
To introduce a quarrel between students and professor
items.explanation: The blunt opening sentences pile up failures, so the professor’s remark about failures being data lands as a hopeful reframing. Nothing shows the students dislike the class, since they laugh and copy her line. The experiments’ design is never explained, and the professor and students never quarrel in the passage.
